A hexamap is a heatmap of age-period-cohort (APC) data drawn with hexagonal
tiles, one per age-period cell. This vignette shows how to prepare the data,
draw a hexamap, and adjust it. The `vignette("apc-patterns")` vignette shows
how age, period and cohort effects look on a hexamap, and
`vignette("overdose")` works through the example of Jalal and Burke (2020).

```{r setup}
library(hexamap)
```

## Why hexagons

In a traditional Lexis diagram, periods run along the x axis and ages along
the y axis, so cohorts (birth years, `period - age`) run along the diagonal.
Relative to age and period, the square grid compresses the distance between
adjacent cohorts by about 30% ($1 - \sqrt{2}/2$), stretches the distance
between cells of the same cohort by about 41% ($\sqrt{2} - 1$), and makes
adjacent cells of a cohort touch only at a corner.

On a hexagonal grid, the three APC axes are at equal 60° angles and
neighboring cells share a full edge along each of them. The grey tiles below
show one cell and its isolines on each grid.

```{r mesh, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Two small grids. On the square Lexis grid, cohort isolines are diagonals and the highlighted cell touches its cohort neighbours only at corners. On the hexagonal grid, age, period and cohort isolines meet at 60 degree angles and the highlighted tile shares an edge with its neighbours on every axis."}
mesh <- matrix(1, nrow = 5, ncol = 5, dimnames = list(1:5, 1:5))
mesh[3, 3] <- 2
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
lexis_map(mesh, color_map = c("grey94", "grey60"), hex_border = "white",
          hex_border_width = 2, isoline_interval = 1, legend = FALSE,
          line_color = "grey30", title_text = "Square tiles")
hexamap(mesh, color_map = c("grey94", "grey60"), hex_border = "white",
        hex_border_width = 2, isoline_interval = 1, legend = FALSE,
        line_color = "grey30", title_text = "Hexagonal tiles")
```

Each tile is centered at

$$x = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} p, \qquad y = a - \frac{p}{2},$$

for age $a$ and period $p$, so neighboring tiles are one age or period group
apart along every axis. `apc_to_xy()` returns these coordinates.

## The data

`hexamap()` takes a numeric matrix with **ages as rows and periods as
columns**, as produced by the NCI APC web tool or SEER\*Stat. Age and period
groups must have the same width (for example single years, or 5-year groups
with 5-year periods). If the matrix has numeric row and column names, the
first age, first period and group width are taken from them:

```{r data}
dim(overdose_white_men)
overdose_white_men[1:4, 1:5]
```

Otherwise, give them with `first_age`, `first_period` and `interval`.

Data in long format, with one row per age and period, can be converted with
`as_apc_matrix()`. Missing combinations become `NA`:

```{r long}
long <- expand.grid(age = seq(20, 80, by = 10), period = seq(1980, 2020, by = 10))
long$rate <- with(long, exp(age / 25) * (1 + (period - 1980) / 40))
rates_10y <- as_apc_matrix(long, value = "rate")
rates_10y
```

and `apc_rates()` computes rates from matrices of counts and population.

## A first hexamap

```{r first, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Hexamap of drug overdose death rates among white men, ages 15 to 70, 1999 to 2018, with age, period and cohort isolines every 10 years."}
hexamap(overdose_white_men, scale_units = "Deaths per 100,000")
```

Isolines are drawn every 10 years here: by default, `hexamap()` picks a round
spacing that gives at most 8 isolines, starting at the first round age and
period. The labels `A:`, `P:` and `C:` mark the age, period and cohort
isolines.

## Isolines and labels

- `isoline_interval`, `first_age_isoline` and `first_period_isoline` set
  where isolines are drawn; cohort isolines pass through the crossings of the
  age and period isolines.
- `isolines` chooses which isolines to draw.
- `labels` changes the label prefixes.
- `highlight` draws chosen ages, periods or cohorts as highlighted lines.

```{r isolines, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Hexamap with isolines every 5 years labelled with full words, and the 1975 birth cohort and the year 2015 highlighted in white."}
hexamap(overdose_white_men,
        isoline_interval = 5,
        labels = c(age = "Age ", period = "", cohort = "Born "),
        highlight = list(cohort = 1975, period = 2015, col = "white", lwd = 2),
        colorbar_range = c(0, 40),
        scale_units = "Deaths per 100,000")
```

By default, cohort labels wrap around the bottom of the hexamap. With
`wrap_cohort_labels = FALSE`, all cohort isolines start on the left edge.

## Colors

`palette` takes `"jet"` (the default, as in the paper) or any palette from
`grDevices::hcl.pals()`, such as the perceptually uniform `"viridis"`;
`color_map` takes any vector of colors. `colorbar_range` fixes the limits;
values outside them get the end colors.

`colorbar_scale` maps values to colors on a `"linear"`, `"log"` or
`"quantile"` scale. On the quantile scale each color covers the same share of
cells, which brings out patterns in skewed data; the colorbar then shows
percentiles on the left.

```{r scales, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Two hexamaps of the overdose data, one with the viridis palette on a log scale and one with the jet palette on a quantile scale with percentiles on the colorbar."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hexamap(overdose_white_men, palette = "viridis", colorbar_scale = "log",
        title_text = "viridis, log scale")
hexamap(overdose_white_men, colorbar_scale = "quantile",
        title_text = "jet, quantile scale")
```

For ratios or differences, `midpoint` gives a diverging scale centered on a
value, with limits symmetric around it. Here, each age's rate is divided by
its rate in 2010:

```{r ratio, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Hexamap of rate ratios relative to 2010 on a blue-white-red diverging log scale centered at 1. Rates are lower than in 2010 before 2010 and higher after, most strongly after 2015."}
ratio <- overdose_white_men / overdose_white_men[, "2010"]
hexamap(ratio, colorbar_scale = "log", midpoint = 1,
        scale_units = "Rate ratio\nvs 2010")
```

## Missing cells

Cells with `NA` are drawn in `na_color` (light grey by default), with a key
below the colorbar labelled `na_label`. In `overdose_white_men`, cells with 9
or fewer deaths are missing because CDC WONDER does not allow publishing
them. Use `na_color = NA` to leave missing cells blank.

## Layouts and annotations

`hexamap()` returns, invisibly, the layout it drew. `hexamap_layout()`
computes the same object without drawing it. The layout holds one row per
cell, with its age, period, cohort, value, coordinates and color, along with
the isolines and the color scale:

```{r layout}
lay <- hexamap_layout(overdose_white_men, colorbar_range = c(0, 40))
lay
head(lay$cells)
```

Draw a layout with `plot()`, and add annotations at any age and period with
`apc_to_xy()`:

```{r annotate, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Hexamap of the overdose data with a white point marking the cell with the highest rate."}
plot(lay, scale_units = "Deaths per 100,000")
peak <- lay$cells[which.max(lay$cells$value), ]
points(apc_to_xy(peak$age, peak$period), pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 1.5)
peak[, c("age", "period", "cohort", "value")]
```

## Lexis diagrams

`lexis_map()` draws the same data on square tiles with the same options,
which makes side-by-side comparisons easy:

```{r lexis, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "A Lexis diagram and a hexamap of the overdose data side by side."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
lexis_map(overdose_white_men, colorbar_range = c(0, 40), legend = FALSE,
          title_text = "Lexis diagram")
hexamap(overdose_white_men, colorbar_range = c(0, 40), title_text = "Hexamap")
```

## ggplot2

`gg_hexamap()` returns a ggplot object, and `autoplot()` draws a layout. A
named list of matrices gives one panel per element, with a shared color
scale:

```{r ggplot, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "The overdose hexamap drawn with ggplot2, with a title added with labs()."}
library(ggplot2)
gg_hexamap(overdose_white_men, colorbar_range = c(0, 40),
           scale_units = "Deaths per\n100,000") +
  labs(title = "Drug overdose deaths, white men")
```

## Saving figures

Hexamaps are taller than wide when there are more ages than periods, as in
most mortality and incidence data. The plot keeps a 1:1 aspect ratio and
fits the device, so choose the device size to match, for example
`png("hexamap.png", width = 5, height = 6.5, units = "in", res = 300)`.

## Code from the paper

The eAppendix of Jalal and Burke (2020) called `create_hexamap()`. That
function is kept, with its argument names, so the published code runs
unchanged:

```{r eappendix, eval = FALSE}
create_hexamap(data = data, first_age = 15, first_period = 1999, interval = 1,
               first_age_isoline = 20, first_period_isoline = 2000,
               isoline_interval = 10, color_scale = c(0, 40))
```

## Reference

Jalal H, Burke DS. Hexamaps for age-period-cohort data visualization and
implementation in R. *Epidemiology*. 2020;31(6):e47-e49.
<https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000001236>
